facts.value: Confucius had a major impact on ancient China’s view of justice and law. Confucius and his disciples believed a harmonious society depended on five relationships: ruler and subject, husband and wife, father and son, older and younger brother, and friend and friend. They believed that when everyone worked on being a good person, cared for these relationships, and fulfilled their responsibilities, society wouldn’t need strict laws or punishments.
facts.programme_association: Justice Studies Major – Bachelor of Science

facts.value: The imperial Chinese code during the Qin dynasty (221-206 BCE) rejected Confucius’ teachings in favor of Legalism, which taught that humans were naturally violent. Legalism taught that to prevent humans from falling into their natural, evil state, the government needed to take full control.
facts.programme_association: Justice Studies Major – Bachelor of Science

facts.value: Li Si, the counselor to the first emperor, created a harsh code following the unification of China. The emperor appointed district officials who served as judges and investigators. Those accused of crimes were guilty until proven innocent, and trials didn’t have lawyers or juries. Punishments varied based on the crime.
facts.programme_association: Justice Studies Major – Bachelor of Science

facts.value: Punishments were harsh; minor violations could lead to fines, hard labor, beatings, and banishment, while serious crimes could result in mutilations, castration, and death.
facts.programme_association: Justice Studies Major – Bachelor of Science

facts.value: When the Han Dynasty (202 BCE-220 CE) made Confucianism the state philosophy, China’s justice system softened.
facts.programme_association: Justice Studies Major – Bachelor of Science

facts.value: The earliest justice systems were deeply impacted by influential philosophers. Philosophy has continued to play a leading role in how society develops and deploys justice.
facts.programme_association: Justice Studies Major – Bachelor of Science
